enrichment.short_title: Construction adjudicator's award unenforceable after non-compliant appointment under the Scheme

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: IDE Contracting sought to enforce a £161,229.61 adjudicator's award against RG Carter after Mr John Smalley decided a payment dispute.

The contract named Stephen Pratt as adjudicator and provided for CIArb nomination if he could not act; Pratt declined on 12 September 2003 before notice of adjudication, but no post-notice request accompanied by the notice was made to him.
RG Carter participated under a jurisdiction reservation, raised appointment defects, withdrew on 31 October 2003, and did not submit to Mr Smalley's jurisdiction ruling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 / summary judgment application in the TCC to enter judgment and enforce a construction adjudicator's award.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; adjudicator lacked jurisdiction because appointment procedure under the Scheme was not complied with and the defendant had not submitted to jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Where a named adjudicator has already indicated unwillingness or inability to act, the referring party must still follow the Scheme by serving notice of adjudication first and then requesting the named person (accompanied by a copy of the notice) unless unwillingness has been communicated to all parties; bypassing that procedure invalidates appointment unless the responding party submits to jurisdiction, and actual prejudice is not required.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Smalley was validly appointed after Mr Pratt's pre-notice refusal
Whether non-compliance with Scheme appointment provisions deprived the adjudicator of jurisdiction
Whether RG Carter submitted to the adjudicator's jurisdiction
Whether the defendant suffered prejudice from the irregular appointment

notes: Long commercial court marine insurance trial; multiple independent grounds for insurer success clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Floating casino vessel claim defeated by overvaluation, warranty breach and fraudulent devices
key_facts: The Game Boy vessel was damaged by an underwater explosion at Avlis shipyard, Greece on 13 January 1999 while laid up for conversion to a floating casino.
Assureds GVC SA sought US$1.8m total-loss indemnity under a marine policy; Eagle Star contended the vessel was worth about scrap value and supporting purchase/charter documents were fabricated.
The insurer also alleged breach of Salvage Association lay-up warranties (no continuous watchman/telephone) and use of fraudulent devices during the claims investigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial on cross-claims for declarations as to marine policy liability after total loss of insured vessel.
enrichment.outcome: Insurer's declarations granted and assureds' indemnity claim dismissed on misrepresentation/avoidance, breach of warranty, and fraudulent devices grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Material overvaluation of an insured vessel can induce avoidance of the policy; ongoing Salvage Association recommendations incorporated into the policy must be complied with throughout the risk period; and an insured who knowingly submits inauthentic documents to embellish a genuine claim during insurer investigation uses a fraudulent device that defeats the claim under Agapitos v Agnew even if the underlying loss occurred.
legal_issues: Whether the vessel's declared $1.8m value was a material misrepresentation inducing cover
Whether the policy covered the vessel at Avlis at the time of loss
Whether lay-up warranties requiring watchman and telephone were breached
Whether assureds used fraudulent devices in presenting MOA, charterparty and valuation documents

enrichment.short_title: Company refused permission to revise filed accounts to remove Part 36 offer reference

statutes_considered.title: Companies (Revision of Defective Accounts and Report) Regulations 1990

key_facts: Company A filed 2002 accounts that gave a true and fair view but included notes referring to a £25m TCC claim and a Part 36 settlement offer without legal advice.
Claimants in the underlying litigation demanded revised accounts omitting the Part 36 reference; the Registrar required a court application.
Company A sought permission under alleged inherent jurisdiction to file substituted accounts, arguing Rush & Tompkins protected without-prejudice settlement references from public disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for permission to file revised company accounts omitting references to Part 36 without-prejudice negotiations.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no inherent jurisdiction to permit revision where statutory filing duties were properly performed and accounts were true and fair.
enrichment.ratio: Limited companies and the Registrar operate under statute; where filed accounts comply with the Companies Act and give a true and fair view, the court has no general inherent supervisory jurisdiction to require removal of extraneous material such as a Part 36 reference, and Rush & Tompkins does not extend to permit revision of publicly filed accounts merely because they disclose without-prejudice negotiations.
legal_issues: Whether the court has inherent jurisdiction to permit filing of revised accounts omitting Part 36 references
Whether without-prejudice privilege protects settlement references in filed company accounts
Whether section 245 voluntary revision procedures or the 1990 Regulations assist the application
Whether discretion would in any event refuse revision on the facts

notes: Landmark unsafe conviction judgment with detailed expert evidence review; convictions quashed at start of reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Cannings murder convictions quashed over unsafe expert evidence on multiple infant deaths
key_facts: Angela Cannings was convicted of murdering two infant sons, Jason and Matthew, after three of her four children died in infancy and earlier ALTE episodes occurred.
The Crown case relied on a pattern of smothering; the defence attributed the deaths to natural SIDS/cot death, supported by fresh post-trial expert evidence and possible genetic factors.
Professor Sir Roy Meadow gave expert evidence; the appeal followed controversy over similar multiple-death prosecutions including Sally Clark and Trupti Patel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against two murder convictions after convictions quashed on 10 December 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; murder convictions quashed as unsafe; court issued guidance on prosecuting multiple unexplained infant deaths.
enrichment.ratio: Where two or more sudden unexplained infant deaths in one family are followed by reputable expert disagreement and natural causes cannot be excluded as a reasonable possibility, prosecution for murder should not proceed unless there is additional cogent extraneous evidence of deliberate harm; convictions resting almost exclusively on such expert conflict are unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether convictions for smothering Jason and Matthew were safe on the expert evidence
Whether rarity of multiple infant deaths in one family proves unlawful killing
How fresh medical and genetic evidence affected the Crown's pattern-based case
What prosecution approach should apply to multiple SIDS cases

enrichment.short_title: Liquidator granted capped income access but denied free use of disputed caravan park sale proceeds
key_facts: Local London Residential Ltd owned a Guildford caravan park purchased for a disputed price amid Mitchell family divorce and bankruptcy litigation.

After winding-up and Barclay Applegate relief letting the liquidator take rental income, competing claims arose from Lisa Mitchell, Sean Mitchell's trustee in bankruptcy, and creditors over beneficial ownership.
The liquidator sought further relief to use sale proceeds for liquidation costs and Bromley County Court litigation, having already spent £110,000 of diverted income.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for further Barclay Applegate-style access to assets claimed outside the liquidation, including future sale proceeds.
enrichment.outcome: Application partially allowed: Lindsay J's income order continued with a £50,000 cap and limited recoupment from sale proceeds if sale occurs before cap reached; no general permission to help herself to sale proceeds.
enrichment.ratio: A liquidator may recover costs of administering and selling property over which title is disputed from income generated by that property, but cannot without more treat disputed sale proceeds as available to fund ownership litigation; creditors should normally be approached to fund contested claims where company assets are uncertain.
legal_issues: Whether the liquidator could access proceeds of sale of the caravan park
Which liquidation and investigation costs were recoverable from disputed assets
Whether the liquidator should have sought a creditor fighting fund
How Barclay Applegate relief should apply pending beneficial ownership trial

enrichment.short_title: Highway authority owes no common law duty to salt trunk roads against hoar frost after Goodes
key_facts: Mr Sandhar died on an icy A428 trunk road in Bedfordshire on 22 December 1996 after hoar frost formed; the road had not been salted beforehand.
Bedfordshire's duty engineer relied on Met Office forecasts and did not use the Icelert system; a salting lorry was dispatched only after police reports of accidents.
Following Goodes v East Sussex CC, claimants argued a common law negligence duty to prevent ice under section 62 improvement powers and the national TRMM winter maintenance scheme.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench Division full trial as lead test case on common law duty of care for precautionary salting after House of Lords decision in Goodes.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the defendant; no common law duty of care to prevent hoar frost or remove ice under the exercised improvement powers.
enrichment.ratio: After Goodes, transient natural hazards such as hoar frost are not within the maintenance duty under section 41 and the Highways Act policy does not impose a common law duty of care to exercise section 62 improvement powers to salt roads; establishing TRMM and delegated trunk-road winter maintenance does not create proximity or a Caparo duty to compensate road users for operational failures to salt.
legal_issues: Whether a highway authority owes a common law duty to prevent ice forming after Goodes
Whether section 62(2) improvement powers support liability for failure to salt
Whether the TRMM winter maintenance scheme creates reliance or proximity
Whether Mr Chandler's failure to use Icelert would have breached any such duty

notes: Clear Court of Appeal decision reversing strike-out in GLO child abuse litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Parallel child abuse claim restored after disproportionate GLO strike-out
key_facts: Taylor brought individual proceedings against Nugent Care Society in 2001, about two and a half years after the cut-off to join the North-West Child Abuse GLO.
His late application to join the GLO was refused by District Judge Fairclough and he did not pursue his appeal before Poole J.
Moses J struck out the individual claim as abuse of process, holding it would undermine GLO discipline and fairness to other claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal civil appeal against strike-out for abuse of process after refusal of out-of-time joinder to a group litigation order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim restored with stay pending directions from the GLO managing judge; strike-out held disproportionate.
enrichment.ratio: Claimants are not obliged to join a GLO, and refusal of late joinder does not automatically make separate proceedings an abuse; striking out is disproportionate where the court can stay parallel proceedings, bind the claimant to generic GLO decisions, and protect defendants on costs instead of barring the claim entirely.
legal_issues: Whether proceeding individually after failed GLO joinder is abuse of process
Whether strike-out was a proportionate response
What case management orders can protect defendants and the GLO without dismissing the claim
How fairness to other GLO claimants affects the decision

notes: Detailed Chancery appeal on lease forfeiture and section 141 LPA 1925 with clear four-ground analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Purchaser's pre-registration re-entry validly forfeited sublease and defeated rent arrears claim
key_facts: Rother bought the head lease of Hanover House in 1999 but was not registered as proprietor until 31 December 2001, unaware of the registration defect.
On 18 July 2000, before registration, Rother peaceably re-entered and forfeited the defendants' sublease for rent arrears and granted a new sublease.
Rother sued for pre-possession rent arrears, arguing the forfeiture was ineffective until registration so section 141 vested accrued rent in the reversioner on registration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery appeal from county court preliminary issue on legal effect of purported forfeiture before Land Registry registration of the head lease.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; sublease treated as forfeited on 18 July 2000 and Rother could not recover pre-possession arrears under section 141.
enrichment.ratio: A purchaser of a leasehold reversion who peaceably re-enters before registration may be presumed to have authority from the transferor, is estopped from denying the forfeiture was effective, and cannot rely on lack of legal title to take advantage of its own wrong and recover rent under section 141 LPA 1925 after later registration.
legal_issues: Whether peaceable re-entry before registration of the head lease forfeited the sublease
Whether presumption of authority or estoppel validated the forfeiture
Whether section 141 vested accrued rent in Rother on 31 December 2001
Whether feeding estoppel retrospectively validated forfeiture without altering the section 141 vesting date

enrichment.short_title: Consultancy claim struck out after adjournment refused over dissolved Irish company
key_facts: Salamony claimed £150,000 for oral consultancy services said to have been performed by Irish company BIM for Balfour Beatty on an Egyptian joint venture in 1995-96.

On the eve of trial Salamony sought adjournment to restore BIM; the judge refused, effectively leaving a claim pleaded in BIM's name bound to fail.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery appeal against refusal of trial adjournment, consequential strike-out, and indemnity costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; adjournment refusal upheld and indemnity costs order justified.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant pursues a hopeless claim in the name of a struck-off company without taking steps to restore it, waits years to commence after disputed breach, and belatedly seeks adjournment on the eve of trial with inconsistent evidence on who contracted, the court may properly refuse adjournment and strike out the claim with indemnity costs.

Whether the claim was bound to fail on its pleaded case

enrichment.short_title: Wall Street Journal denied Reynolds privilege over Saudi bank monitoring terrorism story
key_facts: The Wall Street Journal Europe published a February 2002 article naming the Jameel group among Saudi businesses whose bank accounts were said to be monitored for terrorist ties.
The defendant relied on Reynolds qualified privilege; a jury answered questions rejecting corroboration by sources B to E and finding Mr Munajjed asked for delay before publication.
The judge ruled after Christmas 2003 on whether responsible journalism/public interest justified publication despite defamatory meaning up to reasonable grounds to suspect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling at trial on qualified privilege (Reynolds defence) after jury findings on factual substratum.
enrichment.outcome: Reynolds qualified privilege rejected; publication held not protected despite defamatory meaning.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Lord Nicholls' Reynolds criteria objectively, naming specific businesses as subject to terrorism-related account monitoring was not urgent, breached confidentiality undertakings, lacked reliable corroboration after jury findings, and did not satisfy the duty-interest test for publication to the world at large of defamatory factual allegations about the claimants.
legal_issues: Whether Reynolds qualified privilege applied to publication naming the Jameel group
How jury answers on sources and pre-publication opportunity to comment affected privilege
Whether urgency and public interest justified breaching US-Saudi confidentiality on monitoring
How Bonnick v Morris interacts with privilege where meaning is jury-determined
